title: DNS
objectives: Trace a DNS resolution from cold cache to authoritative server
Reason about TTL and failover trade-offs

sections.markdown: DNS (Domain Name System) is a distributed, hierarchical database that translates domain names (api.example.com) into IP addresses (93.184.216.34).
DNS is your phone's **contacts app**: you remember 'Mom', not her number. DNS lets you remember 'google.com', not an IP that can change anytime.

sections.code:
browser cache -> OS cache -> recursive resolver
  Root server      -> 'ask the .com TLD server'
  .com TLD server  -> 'ask example.com's nameserver'
  Authoritative NS -> 'api.example.com is 93.184.216.34'
  resolver caches the answer for TTL seconds

sections.markdown: TTL is a trade-off: low TTL = faster failover but more DNS traffic; high TTL = better caching but slower changes. Lower TTL hours before a migration so the cutover is fast.

flashcards.back: Recursive does the lookup work on your behalf; authoritative holds the actual records for a zone.

flashcards.front: When can't you use a CNAME?
flashcards.back: At the zone apex (root domain) — use A/ALIAS there instead.
How long a record may be cached before re-querying; controls failover speed vs traffic.

quiz.q: Which server gives the final answer for a domain?
quiz.explain: The authoritative nameserver holds the zone's actual records.

quiz.q: Which record maps a name to an IPv4 address?
quiz.explain: A records map a hostname to an IPv4 address (AAAA for IPv6).

quiz.q: A very low TTL gives you…
options: Faster failover but more DNS traffic
quiz.explain: Short TTLs let changes propagate quickly at the cost of more frequent lookups.
